# SQ5. What are the prospects for more general artificial intelligence?

The past five years have seen much debate on artificial general intelligence (AGI), much of it stemming from a lack of a clear definition of the term.

As former Google AI leader Jeff Dean said, “lots of people have very different definitions of it, and the difficulty of the problem varies by like factors of a trillion.” Some definitions include: a system that can perform any intellectual task a human can, 81 or one that can perform most economically valuable work, or perhaps one that can enter a strange house, locate the kitchen, and make a cup of coffee.

We are left with many questions: What exactly do we mean by general intelligence? Can we predict when it might be developed? Should we encourage or discourage development? Is it enough to scale and refine the current approaches, or is a new approach required?

The so-called “accelerationists” believe that AI progress should continue apace, with the goal of delivering some form of AGI in the near future. Betting markets place a 50% chance of AGI by 2030.

In 2023, over 700 tech leaders and 33,000 people in total signed a letter urging a pause in the development of more powerful AI systems. Many governments discussed issues of regulation, transparency, and sectoral risk. Some regulations temporarily limited access to some services, but there was no pause. The debate arose again in September 2026, following the “rogue AI” incidents described in SQ2: The Decisive Reemergence of Agentic AI, with a number of high-profile industry leaders suggesting a slowdown in development was appropriate. Nevertheless, no pause or obvious slowdown followed.

What could be holding AI systems back? One limitation of LLMs is their focus on language. The hope of many researchers working on physical AI—models trained to sense and act in the real world—is to move beyond cognitively limited models that are able only to manipulate language toward more general models that can sense, plan, and act intelligently. Other limitations of LLMs such as hallucinations may also be tackled by grounding models in the real world. Physical AI and world models are thus seen by some optimistic voices as the missing step needed to get to AGI.

Another important step is the shift from conversational AI toward agentic AI (see also SQ2: The Decisive Reemergence of Agentic AI). Rather than passively waiting for the user to ask a question, agentic AI systems act autonomously. More general artificial intelligence may require this ability to learn and interact with the real world.

Pessimistic voices, by contrast, argue that the transformer architecture, the core neural network technology at the heart of LLMs, will not scale to give us more general artificial intelligence, even with a shift to agentic and physical AI (see Deep Dive Two). If current systems are already trained on all the text on the internet, where is the data for a bigger and better system going to come from? One answer is synthetic data generated by other AI systems, but we don’t know how well that scales. It might simply be too expensive to train more general-purpose models. Frontier models may soon cost billions of dollars to train, and costs at this scale—for models with a lifetime of, say, 18 months—might stretch even the resources of the Silicon Valley giants.

## Limitations of Current AI Models

Researchers at Google introduced the transformer in 2017, 82 and it has since become the foundation for every frontier AI model in use today. The transformer is good at generating fluent language, but not, by itself, as good at reasoning, so modern frontier models augment the basic transformer architecture in at least five ways to achieve more effective reasoning. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) allows the model to retrieve curated documents and analyze how well they address the current problem. Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting encourages the model to write down partial results on a scratchpad and refer back to it (see also SQ2: Reasoning Models). Agentic execution places the model as an orchestrator of tool use (accessing a database, writing and running code, etc.). A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model can get better results with less computational budget by directing each query to a small subpart of the model, rather than using the entire model on every query. Mixture of agents 83 lets the model try to solve a problem in multiple independent ways, and then discuss, vote on, and synthesize a final answer.

Another limitation is the lack of continual learning. An LLM has two sources of memory: the model parameters, which summarize and generalize all that it has learned from its training data, and a context window that covers the current conversation. If the model learns a new skill or a new way of characterizing the world, we’d like to update the parameters so that the model will always have that skill. Theoretically, doing that update is straightforward, but in practice it is difficult. First, a training run can cost millions of dollars, and it is not economically feasible to invest huge sums retraining after every conversation. Second, customers would complain if their private conversations were leaked to other customers. Third, augmenting an existing model is prone to “catastrophic forgetting,” where the model learns a new skill but regresses on an old one. Because of these difficulties, frontier models have not used continual learning.

Finally, models also remain nondeterministic and capricious. Seemingly insignificant changes in the wording of a prompt can result in dramatic changes to the output of the model.
